## Chase the Bad Idea on Purpose to See Where It Runs

A producer describes a move that sounds like sabotage. "I often will think of a bad idea and on purpose try that bad idea just to see where it leads."[^1] Not a good idea he's unsure about. A bad one, tried deliberately. The maker here is named: Rick Rubin. And he reports the results honestly. "Sometimes turns out not to be bad. Sometimes it's worse than I thought."[^1] So the bad idea is genuinely a coin flip — and that's the point. The value isn't in the idea being secretly good. It's in what trying it shows you.

"But the spark of seeing this bad idea through, you start recognizing where it can go."[^1] You run the bad idea, watch what happens, and the watching reveals a direction you couldn't have planned toward. Then comes the operative move. "This is a bad idea, but if this part of it got amplified and if this part of it went away, maybe it's more interesting — and that'll be the next iteration."[^1] Amplify one piece, drop another, and the bad idea becomes the seed of the next attempt. The whole thing is "a series of iterations and looking for clues, looking for bad ideas, strange ideas, dangerous ideas, and seeing what happens."[^1] And the foundation under all of it: "We never know until we try things what works and what doesn't."[^1]

## What This Actually Is

This is a method for generating direction when you don't have one. Normally you try ideas you believe in and avoid ones you don't. Try-the-bad-idea inverts that: you deliberately run an idea you expect to fail, *because the trial produces information the avoidance never would.* A bad idea you never try teaches you nothing. A bad idea you actually execute shows you — in concrete, sensory, undeniable form — exactly why it's bad, and that "why" points at what would be better.

Three things make it more than just "experiment." First, *intentionality* — you pick the bad idea on purpose, not by accident, which means you can do it whenever you're stuck instead of waiting for a mistake. Second, *the iteration loop* — the bad idea isn't the destination; it's input to a refining cycle of amplify-this, drop-that, try again. Third, *the reframe of failure* — when the bad idea turns out worse than expected, that's not a wasted attempt, it's a successful measurement. You now know one direction is dead, and you know it for real, not in theory.

The deepest claim is the foundation sentence: *we never know until we try.* This is an epistemological stance about creative work. Knowing-in-advance is treated as an illusion — and worse, a contaminated one, because any sense that you already know "is only going to be massively informed by these internal biases and well-worn patterns in your mind."[^1] The bad idea is a way to act *before* the biased foreknowledge can rule out the territory.

## The Bad Idea as a Probe That Maps Dead Ground

Why try something you expect to fail? Because the only way to know what an idea actually does is to run it, and the bad idea is the cheapest probe into territory your judgment has pre-marked as worthless. Your judgment is exactly the thing the source distrusts — "massively informed by internal biases and well-worn patterns."[^1] So the regions your taste rules out without testing are precisely the regions most shaped by your blind spots. The bad idea is a flashlight pointed there.

Run the probe and one of two things happens, both useful. It "turns out not to be bad" — your judgment was wrong, and you've found something you'd have skipped forever. Or it's "worse than I thought" — and now you know, concretely, where a wall is. Either way the trial converts a guess into a fact. The producer's "you start recognizing where it can go" is this conversion happening in real time: executing the idea makes its trajectory visible in a way that contemplating it never could.

Then the loop. "If this part got amplified and this part went away."[^1] The bad idea is decomposed — it's never uniformly bad; it has parts. Some part of it had a flicker; some part dragged it down. You amplify the flicker, drop the drag, and run it again. The next iteration is better not because you got smarter in the abstract but because the last trial gave you specific clues. The series of iterations is a search, and the bad ideas are how you sample regions of the space that pure planning would never visit. You're not looking for the bad idea to be good. You're mining it for direction.

This also explains why the move requires *seeing it through* — "the spark of seeing this bad idea through."[^1] A bad idea abandoned at the thought stage gives nothing; the clue lives in the execution. You have to actually make the worse version to read where it points. Trial is the instrument; the idea is just what you feed it.

## Synergies & Handshakes

Try-the-bad-idea is the *action* that [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/the-vacant-mind-asks-for-inspiration|The Vacant Mind Asks for Inspiration]] needs but can't supply on its own. The vacant mind protects inspiration when it arrives. But when nothing arrives — when the channel is dry — you can't just sit vacant forever. The bad idea is what you do in the drought: act anyway, run a probe, generate clues. The two are complementary halves of the same Rubin source: protect the inspiration you get, and manufacture direction when you get none.

It is also the resolution to a tension this source leaves open between non-interference and iteration. The vacant-mind painter says *don't interfere*. The bad-idea producer says *interfere on purpose, repeatedly.* The reconciliation is temporal: don't interfere in the first landing of an inspiration; do iterate aggressively across later versions when you're searching for one. Try-the-bad-idea is the licensed interference — deliberate tampering in service of finding direction.

It pairs with [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/wu-wei-effortless-action|Wu Wei — Effortless Action]] in a way that looks contradictory and isn't. Wu Wei says don't force. The bad idea looks like forcing — but it's the opposite. Forcing is gripping one predetermined outcome. The bad idea is *releasing* the grip on outcome entirely: you try something with no investment in its success, purely to see what happens. That non-attachment to the result is Wu Wei wearing work clothes.

And it bypasses exactly the apparatus [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/critic-blocks-creativity|The Critic Blocks Creativity]] describes. The critic's whole function is to rule ideas out before trial. Try-the-bad-idea overrules the critic by acting before it can veto — and then uses the trial's result as better data than the critic's prediction.

## Analytical Case Study

The producer's account is a complete, compact methodology, and its structure rewards close reading. It opens with the foundation: "We never know until we try things what works and what doesn't."[^1] That's the axiom — foreknowledge is unavailable. Then the move: "I often will think of a bad idea and on purpose try that bad idea just to see where it leads."[^1] Note "on purpose" and "just to see where it leads" — intentional, and aimed at *learning direction*, not at success.

Then the honest results table: "Sometimes turns out not to be bad. Sometimes it's worse than I thought."[^1] Crucially, *both* outcomes are reported as fine. A method that only worked when the bad idea turned out good would be wishful. This one extracts value from the worse-than-expected case too — because "the spark of seeing this bad idea through, you start recognizing where it can go."[^1] The recognition is the yield, independent of the idea's quality.

Then the decomposition-and-iteration engine: "if this part of it got amplified and if this part of it went away, maybe it's more interesting — and that'll be the next iteration."[^1] The idea is treated as separable into parts with different value. The output isn't a verdict (good/bad) but a *next move* (amplify, drop, retry). And the framing of the whole: "a series of iterations and looking for clues, looking for bad ideas, strange ideas, dangerous ideas, and seeing what happens."[^1] Bad, strange, dangerous — the search deliberately includes the regions taste excludes.

The narrator then adds the epistemic kicker, generalizing the producer's practice: instead of asking "is this good enough," "accept that you don't know before you try it. And any sense that you do know already is only going to be massively informed by these internal biases and well-worn patterns in your mind."[^1] This is the case's spine. The bad idea is not a quirk of one producer's personality. It's an operationalization of a claim about knowledge — that creative judgment is biased toward the well-worn, and the only correction is trial in the territory the bias avoids.

## Implementation Workflow AS A SCENE

You're stuck. The good ideas have run out and the work is sitting there refusing to move. Instead of staring harder, you reach for the worst idea in the room — the one your taste flinches at, the obviously-wrong move, the version you'd be embarrassed to show anyone. You don't talk yourself out of it. You build it.

Halfway through making the bad version you feel the flinch confirmed — yes, this is bad. But you keep going, because the clue isn't in the flinch, it's in the finished probe. You see it through. And now you're looking at the actual thing, not the idea of it, and something jumps out: this *part* is dead, but that *part* — that one corner — has a strange charge you didn't expect. The bad idea, fully executed, just pointed at something.

So you take it apart. Amplify the corner with the charge. Drop the dead weight. Run it again. The next version is built from the clue the bad one gave you. Maybe it's still not right — fine, it's another probe, another clue. You're not failing; you're sampling. You keep this up — bad ideas, strange ones, dangerous ones — each one a flashlight into ground your judgment had blacked out, each iteration carrying forward the part that flickered. You never knew until you tried. So you keep trying, on purpose, into the dark.

## The Bad-Idea Failure — Diagnostic Signs

The method has broken down when:

- You only try ideas you secretly believe might be good. That's not trying the bad idea — that's hedged optimism wearing the method's clothes. The information comes precisely from running ideas you expect to fail.
- You abandon the bad idea at the thought stage, satisfied you've "considered" it. The clue lives in the execution; an unexecuted bad idea teaches nothing.
- A worse-than-expected result reads to you as wasted time rather than as a successful measurement of where a wall is. You've kept the old definition of failure and lost the method's whole payoff.
- You run one bad idea, learn nothing instantly, and quit. The method is a *series* of iterations looking for clues — one probe is not the loop.
- You can't decompose a result into parts to amplify and drop — you only render whole verdicts (good/bad). Without the part-level read, there's no next iteration, just a graveyard of rejected wholes.
- Your "search" never visits strange or dangerous territory; every probe stays inside your comfortable taste. Then you're sampling only the regions your bias already approves, which is the exact failure the method exists to fix.

## Evidence, Tensions & Open Questions

The source is one video essay quoting Rubin and adding narrator commentary.[^1] `[PARAPHRASED]` `[POPULAR SOURCE]`. 🚩 SINGLE SOURCE for this specific formulation, and 🚩 MOTIVATED REASONING worth noting — Rubin is a celebrated producer with a commercial and reputational interest in his own method sounding profound; survivorship bias is live (we hear the bad ideas that led somewhere, not the thousands that just wasted studio time). The underlying logic has independent backing — variation-and-selection search, the separation of generation from evaluation, the value of cheap failed experiments — but the source cites none of it and the claim is delivered as personal wisdom.

The central tension is *cost*. Rubin works in a domain (music production) where trying a bad idea is comparatively cheap — a take, an hour, a rerouted plugin. In domains where a single trial is expensive or irreversible (architecture under construction, a surgical approach, a launched product), "try the bad idea on purpose" is reckless, not wise. The method assumes cheap, reversible trials and the source never says so. Open question: how do you get the information benefit of the bad-idea probe when real trials are too costly to run — does simulation, sketching, or small-scale prototyping carry the same clue-yield as full execution, or is the clue specifically lodged in *seeing the real thing through*?

A second tension: the method valorizes "dangerous ideas," but danger and merely-bad are different. Some dangerous ideas are dangerous because they're genuinely generative-but-risky; others are just bad with higher stakes. The source flattens these together. Knowing which dangerous ideas are worth the probe is a judgment the method claims to bypass but probably can't fully escape.

## Author Tensions & Convergences

The narrator (Creative Minds, "Will") presents try-the-bad-idea as a clean illustration of his thesis — bypass the rationalizing, controlling brain; favor action over knowing.[^1] It fits beautifully, maybe too beautifully. He doesn't sit with the fact that this clip is in tension with the vacant-mind painter he quoted minutes earlier, who said *don't interfere* with the inspiration. Rubin's method is structured, repeated interference. The narrator treats both as the same anti-rationalist teaching, and at the level of "bypass the egoic mind" they do converge. But operationally one says protect-and-don't-touch and the other says probe-and-iterate-relentlessly. The convergence is on *trusting action over foreknowledge*; the unexamined split is on *how much you should manipulate the work once it exists.* The narrator never names that the two clips give opposite instructions about interference, which is the most interesting thing about putting them in the same video.

There's also a quiet convergence the narrator gets right without flagging: Rubin's "any sense that you do know already is massively informed by internal biases" is the same distrust-of-the-knowing-mind that runs through the vacant-mind clip and the empty-yourself clip. All three Rubin-adjacent moves treat the confident, knowing, planning mind as the enemy. Try-the-bad-idea is the most *active* expression of that distrust — not emptying the mind to receive, but acting past the mind to learn.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

**Business — [[ARCHIVES/concepts/business/single-piece-feedback-rule-trainability-inversely-correlated|Single-Piece Feedback Rule]].** The business page establishes that tight, fast feedback on small pieces of work drives learning and that the speed of the feedback loop matters more than the size of any single attempt. Try-the-bad-idea is the creative-studio instance of exactly this, and the pairing makes the hidden requirement explicit. Rubin's method only works because the loop is *fast and cheap* — try, see, decompose, retry, in hours. The business frame names the variable the artist leaves implicit: feedback-loop latency. The insight that emerges only by holding both: the bad-idea method is not really about courage or anti-perfectionism, as it's usually romanticized — it's about *loop economics*. Its value is a direct function of how cheap and fast a single trial is. Drop the cost of a trial and the bad-idea probe becomes irresistible; raise it and the same method becomes negligent. This dissolves the apparent paradox of why "try bad ideas" is wisdom in a recording studio and malpractice in surgery: it's the same method, run at radically different loop costs. The artist's mystique and the operator's loop-latency metric are describing one underlying mechanic from two sides — and the operator's frame is what tells you *when* the artist's advice applies.

**History — [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/industrial-consolidation-as-selection|Industrial Consolidation as Selection]].** The history page describes a population of firms subjected to selection pressure, where most variants fail and the few that survive define the surviving form — variation generated blindly, selection applied ruthlessly, direction emerging from the wreckage rather than from anyone's plan. Try-the-bad-idea runs the same variation-and-selection logic *inside a single mind*. The bad ideas are deliberately injected variation; seeing them through is the selection trial; amplify-this/drop-that is the inheritance of the surviving traits into the next generation. The pairing produces a genuinely useful reframe: the individual artist iterating on bad ideas is running, at small scale and fast tempo, the same blind-variation-plus-selection process that an entire industry runs slowly across decades of firm births and deaths. The history page shows the process is *impersonal* — no firm "knew" the right form; it emerged from selection. That impersonality is the deep justification for Rubin's distrust of foreknowledge. Just as no planner could have known which firms would survive, no artist can know in advance which idea works — both systems generate knowledge only through trial-and-selection, because the information literally does not exist before the trial. Holding both pages turns "we never know until we try" from a humble aphorism into a structural claim: in any sufficiently complex search space, foreknowledge is not merely biased, it is *unavailable in principle*, and variation-plus-selection is the only process that generates the missing information — whether the search runs across an industry or across an afternoon at the mixing board.

## The Live Edge

**The sharpest implication.** If creative judgment is "massively informed by internal biases and well-worn patterns," then your *taste* — the very faculty you trust most to tell good from bad — is also your most systematic blind spot. The ideas your taste rejects fastest are the ones most shaped by your conditioning, which means the regions you avoid most confidently are the regions where your originality is most likely hiding. Try-the-bad-idea is, read this way, a deliberate program of *betraying your own taste* to escape it. The cruel corollary: the better and more refined your taste becomes, the more confidently it forecloses, and the more disciplined you have to be about violating it on purpose. Mastery doesn't free you from the need for bad ideas. It makes them more necessary, because a stronger taste casts a larger shadow over the territory it won't enter.

**Generative questions.**
- When trials are expensive or irreversible, what carries the clue-yield of a full bad-idea execution? Does a sketch or prototype probe the same territory, or is the clue specifically in seeing the *real* thing through?
- Is there a way to tell a generative dangerous idea from a merely-bad high-stakes one before the trial — or is that distinction exactly what the method refuses to let you make in advance?
- How many bad-idea iterations is the right number before a search should be abandoned? The method has no stopping rule; "looking for clues" could run forever.
- Does the value of try-the-bad-idea decline as a field matures and the cheap-to-probe regions get exhausted, pushing the remaining gains into the expensive, hard-to-trial territory the method handles worst?

## Connected Concepts

- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/the-vacant-mind-asks-for-inspiration|The Vacant Mind Asks for Inspiration]] — protect inspiration when it comes; probe with bad ideas when it doesn't
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/wu-wei-effortless-action|Wu Wei — Effortless Action]] — non-attachment to outcome is what lets you try a bad idea freely
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/critic-blocks-creativity|The Critic Blocks Creativity]] — the bad-idea trial overrules the critic's pre-verdict
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/write-to-discover-paradox|The Write-to-Discover Paradox]] — acting before you know, and learning by doing
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/taste-development-protocol|Taste Development Protocol]] — the faculty that try-the-bad-idea deliberately violates to escape its blind spots
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/frayed-endings-not-knots|Frayed Endings, Not Knots]] — iteration as the path to the finished form

# Daishō — Large and Small

## The Dimmer Switch on Violence: A Gun That Fires the Same Bullet Every Time

A warrior's body does not know how big the threat is. It only knows how to respond. Drop your full force on a drunk at a party and you have killed a man over spilled beer. Hold back when your life is on the line and you die polite. The body, once trained to fight, is a loaded gun — and a gun does not pick a small bullet for a small target. It fires the same round at everyone who pulls the trigger.[^1]

Daishō means "large and small." It is the discipline of choosing the size of your response on purpose, before the body chooses for you. The master metaphor is a dimmer switch. Most trained people have only a light switch: on or off, full force or nothing. The danger is not having too much power. The danger is having no middle.

## What This Actually Is

Daishō names the two swords a samurai carried before the Meiji Restoration — the long katana for the open field and the short wakizashi worn at all times for close work. The two blades demand completely different bodies. The katana is heavy, swung wide with both hands, built for a strong and aggressive spirit. The wakizashi is light, used in one hand, built for small, fast, defensive motion. Many teachers kept students away from the short sword for the first ten or twenty years, afraid it would shrink the student's spirit.[^1]

From those two swords comes a rule with two layers. The small layer: do not use short-sword technique in a long-sword situation, or the reverse — match the tool to the job. The large layer, the one that matters off the mat: never let a small event swallow more attention than it is worth. A minor annoyance and a major battle are different sizes, and you must consciously pick a response that fits.[^1]

The trap is that this sounds too obvious to name. Everybody knows you don't kill a guest because he had one too many. But "everybody knows" is a statement about minds. The body of a warrior is not a mind. It is a finely tuned machine, cocked and loaded with the safety off, and it does not care what manner of man pulls its trigger.[^1] The whole point of daishō is that the obvious thing the mind knows is exactly the thing the trained body forgets.

## Filling the Space: The Internal Logic

Here is the mechanism. A trained body has one default — maximum output — because that is what survival rehearsal built into it. The reflex fires at full size whether the threat is full-size or trivial. So the work of daishō is not building more power. It is building a deliberate brake on power.

Lovret's instruction for applying it is almost embarrassingly simple: let your spirit fill all the available space, and no more.[^1] If the space is a war, your spirit grows large and you reach for large strategies automatically. If the space is a small room or a drunk at a party, you let your spirit stay small, and small techniques follow on their own. You are not calculating force in your head. You are setting the size of the container and letting the response pour itself to fit.

This is why the gun metaphor cuts both ways. A gun is reliable precisely because it does not modulate — same bullet every time. That reliability is a virtue in combat and a catastrophe in a living room. The soldier's body has been engineered into a gun, and daishō is the conscious act that gives the gun a dimmer switch it does not naturally have. Lovret is blunt about the cost: by thinking small, the soldier restricts his automatic reflexes. This slows his response to a real emergency. He is trading speed for proportion, accepting that he will be a half-second late to the rare large fight in exchange for not destroying the common small one. He "puts his spirit in a straitjacket in order to live within the rules of society. He becomes a killer who does not kill."[^1]

The reverse failure matters just as much. A small matter that captures your full attention is a tactical hole. Tap an inexperienced fighter on the nose, just hard enough to draw blood, and the trivial injury floods his attention — leaving you free to do whatever you actually need while he fixates on the trickle.[^1] Over-responding to the small thing does more than waste effort. It blinds you to the large thing forming behind it.

## Information Emission (Synergies & Handshakes)

Daishō is not a solo principle; it leaks into how you read and steer other people, and that emission is where its reach widens.

Because attention has a fixed size, you can manipulate an opponent's by managing yours. Lovret links daishō to *utsurakashi* — moving your sword tip in a small, light, random, fast pattern. The opponent's mind copies the motion. He starts taking small fast steps, stops thinking big, drifts into short-sword technique, and opens himself to one powerful large attack.[^1] You have shrunk his spirit by showing him a small picture. This is the same gear that runs *shidai*, the circumstances of battle: the right response size is read off the situation, and the situation can be edited.

The principle also emits straight into institutions. Lovret's flat line — "the business of business is business" — is daishō at organizational scale. Customer relations, employee relations, community relations are all short-sword matters; they must serve the long sword of profit and survival or be set aside. A company that lets small, emotional matters take precedence "may be well loved but it will not be long-lived. Through constant attention to the short sword, the long sword rusts in its sheath."[^1] An army emits the same way in reverse: dig the beachhead foxhole too deep, spend too long consolidating, and the enemy recovers — small thinking in a large situation, a pause treated as a strategy.[^1]

## Analytical Case Study: The Killer Who Does Not Kill

Take Lovret's own hardest example and follow it all the way down. A soldier spends long enough on the front line that battle becomes ordinary. His body learns the gun-default: threat means maximum output, no deliberation, no dimmer. This is exactly what kept him alive. The reflex that fires full-size at any trigger is the most valuable thing the training built.[^1]

Then the war ends and you try to put that body back into a society with rules. The problem is now visible as a structural one, not a moral one. The man's mind knows you do not destroy a guest who had too much to drink. But the body that learned the front line is not governed by the mind's knowing. It is a loaded gun that fires the same bullet at the drunk that it fired at the enemy. Lovret notes the institutional consequence directly: soldiers hardened by the front line require a cool-down period before they can be released back into society.[^1] That cool-down is not therapy in the modern sense — it is the re-installation of a dimmer switch the war removed.

Daishō is the method for that re-installation. The soldier deliberately thinks small. He restricts his automatic reflexes by conscious act of will, accepting that this slows him in a true emergency, because the slowing also caps his response to the thousand minor frictions of ordinary life. He straitjackets his own spirit on purpose. The result is the paradox in the title: a killer who does not kill — a man who keeps the full capacity but holds the brake himself, every waking hour, because nothing else will hold it for him.[^1]

The worked lesson is that re-socialization is not the deletion of capacity. It is the re-acquisition of proportion. The dangerous veteran is not the one who can kill — every veteran can. The dangerous one is the one whose switch is stuck on, who has lost the small-sword setting entirely, whose body answers every annoyance at the size of a war. And the same diagnosis runs the other way for the under-trained civilian, who has no large setting at all and panics at a nosebleed. Health, in this frame, is range: a body that can deliberately choose any size between off and full, and choose the one that fits.

## Implementation Workflow: Sizing the Response

You are in a small room. The walls are close, the ceiling low, a single bulb. A man stands across from you with a long blade, and his style is built for open ground — wide, two-handed, sweeping. You feel your own body wanting to answer at full size, to meet his big technique with your own. You stop that. You let your spirit shrink to the size of the room. Not the size of the war you trained for — the size of *this* space, these four walls.

You feel the change physically. Your stance pulls in. Your steps go short and quick. You discard the long blade — it would only tangle in the close air — and you draw the short one. The room that traps his sweeping cuts is the room your small techniques were made for. His large strategy snarls on the surroundings; yours moves clean in the gaps.[^1]

Now a different scene. A party. A drunk leans into your space, loud, harmless, a minor annoyance wearing the costume of a threat. The gun-body wants to fire. You do not let your spirit fill the war-sized container it defaults to. You let it fill only the actual space: one rude man, one small problem, a fraction of your attention. You feel yourself refuse to give him more notice than he has earned, because you know the cost of fixation — that while you stare at the nosebleed in front of you, the real situation forms unwatched behind your back. You give the small matter its small share, no more, and keep the rest of your attention wide.

Both scenes are the same act. You do not calculate force. You set the size of the container — the room, the war, the drunk — and you let your response pour itself to fit. Large container, large strategy, automatically. Small container, small technique, instinctively. You precisely fit the situation because you sized the situation first.[^1]

## The Stuck-Switch Failure: Diagnostic Signs

You can name the failure by its symptoms. The first sign is having only on and off — no middle setting. The person meets every conflict at one volume, usually maximum, because that is the only setting the training left intact. Ask them to respond small and they cannot; the dimmer was never installed or has rusted shut. This is the hardened soldier in the living room and, scaled up, the army that knows only the all-out advance.

The second sign is the mirror: over-responding to small matters. A trivial annoyance captures full attention. The nosebleed floods the whole mind. The company pours itself into employee feelings and community goodwill while the long sword of survival rusts in the sheath.[^1] Watch for the person, team, or institution whose attention size never matches the event size — who treats the drunk like a war and, having spent everything on the war that wasn't, has nothing left when the real one arrives. Both signs are the same defect: a body or an organization that cannot consciously choose the size of its own response.

## Evidence / Tensions / Open Questions

The source is a single practitioner-popular manual, and the central claim — that battle-hardened bodies fire at one default size and need a deliberate cool-down to re-enter society — is asserted as lived craft knowledge, not measured.[^1] It rhymes hard with what is now discussed under combat-stress reactions and the difficulty of demobilizing trained soldiers, but Lovret offers no data, only the swordsman's testimony. Treat it as a sharp practitioner model rather than a verified finding. [POPULAR SOURCE]

A genuine tension sits inside the doctrine. Lovret says large strategies are preferable for spiritual development, and that teachers fear the short sword shrinks the spirit — yet the whole technology of daishō is the deliberate restriction of the spirit to small size.[^1] So is shrinking the spirit a danger or the discipline? The page does not resolve this, and it should not: the small sword is a developmental hazard *and* the only tool for living in society, both at once.

Open question: the cool-down for soldiers is named but never specified. What actually re-installs the dimmer — time, ritual, graded re-exposure to small stakes? Lovret stops at naming the need.

## Author Tensions & Convergences

Lovret is the sole source here, so the tension is internal to one writer rather than between rival authorities. He holds two positions that do not fully reconcile and he does not pretend they do. On one side he prizes the large spirit as the vehicle of spiritual growth and warns that decades of short-sword training stunt a student. On the other he hands the reader a method whose entire purpose is to clamp the large spirit down to small size so a trained body can survive a dinner party. The convergence point is proportion: both the warning and the method serve the same master, which is *fit* — the spirit that is exactly as large as the situation and no larger. Where Lovret is most useful is precisely where he refuses to flatten this. He lets the short sword be both poison and medicine, and he lets the trained body be both the asset that wins wars and the liability that cannot be safely released into peace. The honesty of holding both is what keeps the doctrine from collapsing into a slogan.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

Daishō reaches past swordsmanship into two domains that study the same problem from different angles.

The first handshake is to **psychology**, specifically the re-socialization of hyper-trained reflexes and the question of proportionality. Lovret's "killer who does not kill" is, in clinical language, a body whose threat-response has been conditioned to fire at maximum amplitude regardless of stimulus size — the front-line default that will not stand down. Psychology studies this as the difficulty of demobilizing combat stress: the startle that never recalibrates, the trivial trigger that recruits a war-sized arousal, the veteran whose nervous system kept the gun loaded after the war ended. The structural parallel is exact. Lovret's dimmer-switch metaphor maps onto what a regulated nervous system is supposed to do — scale arousal to the actual threat — and his "stuck on on/off" failure maps onto a dysregulated one that knows only flood or freeze. The insight the connection produces, that neither domain reaches alone, is this: re-socialization is not the removal of capacity but the *re-acquisition of range*. Psychology often frames recovery as reducing reactivity, as if the goal were a quieter system. Lovret's frame insists the soldier keeps his full lethal capacity intact — the cure is not a smaller gun but a working dimmer, the deliberate ability to choose any size on demand. That reframes the therapeutic target from "calm down" to "regain proportion," which is a different and harder thing.

The second handshake is to **behavioral-mechanics**, specifically proportional response and calibrated escalation. In any influence or conflict system — negotiation, deterrence, policing, escalation ladders — the operator's problem is identical to the swordsman's: match the magnitude of your move to the magnitude of the situation, because over-responding burns credibility and resources while under-responding invites the larger blow. Lovret's rule that a small matter must never take more than a fraction of your attention is the same logic that says do not spend your strongest leverage on a trivial dispute, and do not meet a trivial provocation with your heaviest sanction. The structural parallel is the graduated ladder: short sword for small situations, long sword for large, with the explicit warning that a pause in a needed advance is itself a short-sword error in a long-sword moment.[^1] The insight that neither domain produces alone: behavioral-mechanics usually treats escalation as a *choice made in the head*, a deliberate selection from a menu of responses. Lovret adds the bodily substrate behavioral-mechanics tends to ignore — that the trained operator has a *default size* baked into the body, and that calibrated response is not free selection but a fight against a reflex that wants to fire at one fixed amplitude. The dimmer switch is not standard equipment. The operator who thinks he is calmly choosing his escalation may in fact be a gun that only knows one bullet, and daishō's contribution is to make that default visible so it can be overridden on purpose.

## The Live Edge

**The Sharpest Implication.** The dangerous person is not the one with the most force. It is the one with the fewest settings. A trained body, a hardened soldier, an all-or-nothing operator, a company that meets every problem at one volume — each is dangerous precisely because it has lost the middle, not because it is weak. Capacity without a dimmer is the liability. So the real skill, the thing worth decades, is not building a bigger gun. It is building the switch that lets you fire any size of round on command — and remembering that the switch is the part that does not come standard.

**Generative Questions.**
1. If proportion is range and not reduction, what does a true "cool-down" protocol for a hyper-trained person actually consist of — and could it be designed rather than waited out?
2. Where in your own life have you mistaken a stuck-on switch for strength — meeting small annoyances at war-size and calling it intensity?
3. Can an organization install a daishō dimmer deliberately, or do institutions only ever default to one bullet until a crisis forces the other?

## Connected Concepts

- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/cross-domain/the-warrior-as-semi-domesticated-specialist|The Warrior as Semi-Domesticated Specialist]] — the killer-who-does-not-kill is the same figure: full lethal capacity held under deliberate social restraint.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/cross-domain/kokoro-isolated-regiment|Kokoro — The Isolated Regiment]] — the internal posture that lets a trained body hold its own brake.
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/cross-domain/shidai-circumstances-of-battle|Shidai — Circumstances of Battle]] — response size is read off the situation; daishō is how you size the response to those circumstances.

# Tabata's Childhood OBE — High Fever, Soul Looking Down, the Practitioner's Origin

## The Detachment

In one paragraph of Book 10, Tabata names the event that started him:[^1]

> In my childhood, I experienced detachment of my soul from the body while I was suffering from a high fever. To my surprise, my separate self was looking down at my body from above. This mystic experience impelled me to explore the unknown realms. After experimenting with various forms of the martial arts, I finally stepped into the field of karate-do, where no weapons are allowed.[^1]

The disclosure is one of two autobiographical anchors in the entire 4,184-line book — the other is the lineage from Funakoshi through Obata to Tabata's establishment of the North American Karate Federation. The OBE confession is the *interior* origin; the lineage is the *institutional* origin. Both are necessary. The OBE is what made Tabata search. The lineage is where he found what he was looking for.

The phenomenology Tabata describes is one of the standard out-of-body experience reports: the *separate self* (Tabata's phrase, not "soul" or "consciousness" or "I") is *looking down* at the body. The body is below; the experiencer is above. The experiencer is identified as the *self* — Tabata does not write that he "saw his body" but that "my separate self was looking down at my body from above." The grammatical structure preserves the experiential structure: there are two selves, one of them is the *real* self (the one looking), the other is the *body* (which is being looked at).

This is one of the standard NDE/OBE phenomenologies documented across thousands of cases in the modern medical and parapsychological literature. Tabata does not engage with that literature; he reports the experience as personal and lets the reader categorize it.

## What the Experience Did

The functional payload of the experience, as Tabata reports it, is search. The OBE *impelled* him to *explore the unknown realms*. Not to become a Buddhist, not to seek further OBEs, not to develop psychic abilities. To *search*. The search led through "various forms of the martial arts" and terminated in karate-do.

The terminal choice deserves attention. Tabata chose karate-do *specifically because no weapons are allowed*. The weaponless quality is what made the choice. This pairs with the kara=ku claim that the entire Mind Power book argues toward: if kara means emptiness/ku, then karate-do is the *most direct route to ku among the martial arts*, because the practitioner is not mediated by an external instrument. The body alone trains directly into the emptiness. A swordsman trains the sword; a kendoka trains the bamboo blade; an aikidoka trains the throwing of a partner; a karate practitioner trains *only the body* — and through the body, the emptiness the body is.

The OBE confession and the karate-do choice belong together. Tabata at age (unspecified) experienced *not being identified with his body*. The practice he eventually chose is the practice that *uses the body alone to train into the realization that the body is empty*. The choice is consistent with the experience.

## Evidence / Tensions / Open Questions

The OBE is autobiographical and unverifiable from outside. Tabata reports it without specifying age, illness type, duration of the experience, or whether the experience repeated. The single-paragraph disclosure is presented without elaboration — Tabata uses it to motivate the rest of Book 10 (the introduction of the Heart Sutra) and does not return to it.

**Tension on the cultural framing**: OBE/NDE reports vary across cultures in their phenomenology (the tunnel-of-light is more common in Western Christian-influenced contexts; figure-encounters and landscape-features differ across traditions). Tabata's report is bare phenomenology — separate-self, looking-down, body-below — without the cultural overlay. This is either a careful presentation (Tabata deliberately strips the cultural content to make the report cross-cultural) or a brief presentation (Tabata is not interested in elaboration). Either reading is plausible.

**Open question on pattern matching**: Multiple Japanese martial-arts founders and masters have biographical episodes involving illness, near-death, or dissociation as the originating event. Morihei Ueshiba's spiritual awakening was preceded by illness and a profound experience in 1925. Gichin Funakoshi reported transformative encounters during illness. Hakuin Ekaku's *meditative sickness* and recovery is documented. The pattern — practitioner-mystic-origin via a dissociation or near-death event in early life — appears repeatedly. Is this a real cross-practitioner pattern, a confirmation bias in autobiographical literature, or a structural feature of how serious practitioners construct their own origin narratives? Worth filing as META question.

**Tension on "no weapons" framing**: Karate-do is weaponless in the standard practice, but Kobudo (Okinawan weapons traditions) is closely related and was studied by Tabata himself (per Hasumi's foreword line 160: "the in-depth research of etiquette, Okinawan Kobudo, and Zen"). Tabata's *no weapons are allowed* refers to karate-do proper, not to the broader budo ecosystem he inhabits. The framing is precise but easy to over-read — Tabata is not claiming that all weaponed martial arts are less direct routes to ku, only that his choice was for the weaponless one.

## Author Tensions & Convergences

The OBE-as-practitioner-origin pattern, if real, suggests a structural feature of practitioner-mystic biography. The Lowry *Essence of Budo* corpus does not document a comparable origin event for Lowry's own practice. The Tokitsu-on-Musashi corpus implies but does not document the analogous Musashi event (Musashi's mountains-training period suggests dissociation from worldly life but not a single named event). The Stevens-on-Tesshu corpus *does* document a parallel event: Tesshu's March 30, 1880 enlightenment was a discrete moment of dissolution and integration. Tesshu's event came mid-career, after decades of practice; Tabata's came in childhood, before practice. The two are not the same in developmental timing but are structurally similar in phenomenology — the *separate-self* component is present in both.

The cross-domain convergence with creative-practice methodologies is interesting. Several Perell-interview practitioners (Whyte, Karlsson, MacCulloch) report formative experiences that *broke their identification with a particular self-construction* and made their later work possible. Whyte's mountain experience; Karlsson's writing-as-summoning-a-self; MacCulloch's defeat-as-historian-equipment. The structural shape — *a self-rupture early enough to determine the practice that follows* — appears across very different disciplines. Tabata's high-fever OBE is the budo version of this pattern.

The most distant convergence is with the comparative-religion literature on initiatory illness in shamanic traditions. Mircea Eliade documented the pattern: future shamans across Siberia, Central Asia, and the Americas frequently report severe childhood or adolescent illness with dissociation, recovery with new sensitivity, and subsequent vocation. The pattern is universal enough to suggest a structural relationship between illness-induced dissociation and the emergence of practitioner-mystic vocation. Tabata's experience fits the cross-cultural pattern.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

The OBE-as-practitioner-origin sits at the intersection of psychology (dissociation and consciousness), cross-cultural religion (initiatory illness), practitioner-tradition biography (founders' origin narratives), and the wider question of how disciplines select their practitioners. The handshakes below trace where the pattern appears.

- **Psychology / dissociation as developmental gateway**: The OBE is a dissociative event. Modern psychology treats dissociation primarily as pathology (dissociative disorders) but also documents adaptive dissociation in trauma response and meditative states. The handshake reveals: the same neurological capacity that produces dissociative pathology produces the practitioner-mystic-origin experience. The distinction between pathology and gateway depends on what happens *after* the dissociation — whether the practitioner finds a tradition that can hold and develop what the dissociation opened, or whether the practitioner is left alone with an experience the surrounding culture cannot integrate. Tabata's culture (post-war Japan with intact Buddhist and martial-arts traditions) could integrate his experience; a Western child with the same experience in 1950 secular suburbia would likely have had no framework to integrate it and would have either suppressed it or developed it as pathology.

- **Cross-cultural / shamanic initiatory illness**: Eliade's *Shamanism* documents the pattern across Siberia and Central Asia. The handshake produces a generalization: severe childhood illness with dissociation, followed by recovery and vocation, is a near-universal initiatory pattern in traditions that recognize the practitioner-mystic role. Tabata's experience and Japanese-Buddhist reception of it sit inside this wider pattern. The implication: the budo tradition operates with a *shamanic substrate* that most modern practitioners do not name explicitly but that the founding generation often carries.

- **Practitioner-tradition / founders' origin narratives**: Ueshiba's 1925 illness-and-awakening, Funakoshi's transformative episodes, Hakuin's meditative sickness, the broader pattern of Japanese spiritual founders with documented illness-origin events. The handshake reveals: the practitioner-mystic biography is not random. The same structural event recurs because the same neurological / spiritual gateway exists and the same kind of person walks through it. Tabata's contribution is one more data point inside an extensive collection. The collect-set is itself a research target.

- **Creative-practice / self-rupture as practice-precursor**: Several Perell-interview creative practitioners report formative experiences that broke a prior self-construction and made the later work possible. Whyte's *Camino*-mountain rupture; Karlsson's pre-writing-life decade of search; MacCulloch's relationship between personal-identity formation and historical scholarship. The handshake reveals: the *rupture-then-practice* pattern is not specific to martial-mystic traditions. Long disciplined practice in any domain may select for practitioners who have undergone an early rupture, because the rupture-and-search dynamic is what makes the long practice tolerable and meaningful. Tabata's high-fever OBE is the budo instance of a wider creative-practice pattern.

- **Cross-domain / weaponless route as direct route**: The choice of karate-do *because no weapons are allowed* opens a connection to the wider question of which discipline is the *most direct* route to a given destination. Tabata's claim (implicit) is that for someone seeking emptiness, weaponless practice is more direct than weaponed practice because the practitioner is not mediated by an external instrument. The handshake to the Heart Sutra page and to the muto-ryu Tesshu page reveals: the *no-X* moves in Japanese practice (no-sword in muto-ryu, no-weapon in karate-do, no-mind in mushin, no-self in muga) are systematically about *removing the mediating layer between practitioner and destination*. The destination is reached more directly when fewer intermediaries are present. This is a generalizable principle that extends well outside martial arts — disciplines that train the practitioner *via* an instrument always include the instrument as a possible obstacle, while disciplines that train the practitioner *via the body alone* (or *via no body* in some contemplative traditions) remove that obstacle.

## The Live Edge

**The Sharpest Implication**

The contemporary Western secular framework treats childhood OBEs as either (a) pathological dissociation requiring treatment, or (b) neurological epiphenomena of fever-induced brain states, of no further significance. Tabata's case demonstrates a third possibility: the same experience, embedded in a culture with intact practitioner-mystic traditions, *initiates a lifelong vocation* that produces verifiable practitioner outcomes (long teaching career, founding of NAKF, training of thousands of students). The variable is not the experience itself but the culture's capacity to *receive* the experience as initiation rather than as pathology. A culture that loses the practitioner-mystic frameworks loses access to the developmental pathways those frameworks make available. Children who would have become Tabata in a culture that recognized the pattern become diagnostic cases in a culture that does not. This is not just about budo. It is about which experiences a culture treats as gateways and which it treats as symptoms — and which experiences therefore *produce* their cultural reception.

**Generative Questions**

- How many Western children have OBE experiences during childhood illness? The medical literature documents the phenomenon but rarely follows the children into adulthood. Where do the experiences go in a culture without practitioner-mystic frameworks to hold them?
- The Eliade pattern (shamanic initiatory illness) and the Tabata pattern (budo founder origin) and the creative-practice pattern (self-rupture before lifelong work) may be the same pattern across different traditions. If so, what are the *necessary conditions* for the pattern to produce a practitioner rather than a casualty?
- Tabata's *no weapons are allowed* framing suggests that the choice among martial arts is not arbitrary — different routes have different directness to different destinations. Is there a developmental-fit literature in the budo tradition that names *which martial art for which kind of practitioner*, and where does Tabata's choice of karate-do for a child OBE-experiencer fit in that literature?

## Connected Concepts

- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/cross-domain/heart-sutra-as-karate-do-root-text-tabata|Heart Sutra as Karate-Do Root Text]] — the destination the OBE-initiated search led toward
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/muto-ryu-no-sword-doctrine|Muto Ryu — No-Sword Doctrine]] — Tesshu's parallel terminal-state event
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/cross-domain/uchusokuga-universe-equals-self-bridge-doctrine|Uchusokuga — Universe = Self]] — the structural truth the OBE pre-figured
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/cross-domain/musashi-tree-strings-trees-dont-fear-doctrine|Musashi's Tree-Strings]] — Musashi's parallel mountains-practice rupture
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/cross-domain/tanren-as-flame-discipline-tabata|Tanren as Flame-Discipline]] — the practice that channels the post-OBE search into developmental work

# Technology and Moral Distance: How Physical Distance Enables Abstraction and Atrocity

## The Progression of Distance: From Bow to Drone

As warfare technology has evolved, the physical distance between killer and killed has increased. This increasing distance corresponds to increasing abstraction of the target.

A soldier with a bow must see the person they are killing. The person is visible as an individual. They have a face, an expression, a moment of death visible to the killer.

A soldier with a rifle can kill from a distance where the individual is no longer visible as a person — they are a target-shaped object at a distance.

An artillery operator can kill targets specified only by map coordinates. The targets are invisible; they exist only as data points.

A drone operator watches a heat signature on a screen. The target is abstracted to thermal image. The operator sees no face, hears no sound, witnesses no moment of death.

A bomber sees nothing at all. The target is abstract: a building, a city block, a coordinate.

Each step in technological distance corresponds to a step in target abstraction.[^1] And each step of abstraction makes the kill psychologically easier. The more abstract the target, the less empathy is triggered, the less moral constraint is active.

## Technology Enables, Institutions Choose

Crucial distinction: technology *enables* abstraction; it does not *require* it.

A drone can be used to kill from a distance where you witness the consequence (seeing the person after the strike, understanding the harm you caused). Or it can be used to kill from a distance where you see only the abstraction (the thermal signature, the building outline).

An institution *chooses* whether to use the technology to maximize distance and abstraction, or to resist that tendency.

Institutional choice determines whether technology becomes a tool of abstraction-enabling atrocity, or whether it remains under constraints that preserve the visibility and humanity of the target.

This is crucial: you cannot blame technology for atrocity. You can only blame institutional choice to use technology for abstraction.[^1]

## The Mechanism: Dissociation Through Distance

The mechanism works through dissociation. The killer can experience themselves as distant from the kill. The drone operator is physically far away and mediated by technology. They experience their action as button-pressing, not as killing.

The bureaucrat experiences themselves as executing policy, not as causing death. The bomber experiences themselves as completing a mission, not as destroying people.

Distance enables dissociation. Dissociation enables the psychological override of empathy. Empathy is prevented from activating because the killer is not present to the killing.

But dissociation is not automatic. It requires institutional support. An institution must frame distance as appropriate ("you are following orders from a distance"), must reinforce dissociation ("you are operating the equipment, not killing people"), must prevent reintegration of the dissociated experience.

## The Moral Cost of Distance

Distance creates a strange asymmetry: the killer is safe from the target's retaliation (protected by distance), but also safe from the target's visibility (which would trigger empathy).

A person face-to-face with someone they are harming experiences the harm directly. The person's suffering is visible. Their humanity is evident. This visibility creates moral constraint: it becomes difficult to harm someone whose suffering you are witnessing.

But a person separated by distance experiences no such constraint. The target is not visible as suffering. Their humanity is not evident. The moral constraint is not activated.

This is why: institutions prefer distance. Distance is warfare's ultimate technology. Not because distance provides military advantage (though it does), but because distance provides moral advantage — it enables atrocity without triggering the moral constraint that would prevent it.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

### Cross-Domain ↔ Technology/Ethics: Tool Neutrality and Institutional Choice

Technology ethics often debates whether technologies are neutral tools or whether they embed values. This debate is resolved by recognizing: technologies enable specific possibilities, but institutions choose which possibilities to actualize.

A drone is a neutral tool capable of many uses. But an institution that uses drones for surveillance from a distance where they can witness consequences makes different moral choices than an institution using drones to kill from a distance where only thermal images are visible.

The handshake: understanding technology as enabling-but-not-determining allows for realistic engagement. You cannot prevent distance technology (distance is possible). But you can design institutions that constrain how distance is used — that require witnessing consequences, that maintain moral visibility, that resist the tendency to abstract.

### Cross-Domain ↔ Psychology: Dissociation and Mediation

Psychology describes dissociation as a defense mechanism where the psyche separates from direct experience. A person in trauma may dissociate from the pain of the trauma to make it survivable.

Dissociation is normally pathological — it prevents integration and perpetuates trauma. But distance technology enables institutional dissociation — the killer is psychologically distant from the killing even though they are instrumentally causing it.

The handshake: understanding dissociation as a defense mechanism (psychology) and understanding institutional distance (behavioral-mechanics) together reveals: institutions deliberately engineer dissociation to prevent moral constraint from operating.

This suggests: healing requires reintegration — the killer must experience themselves as present to the killing, must witness the consequence, must feel the empathy that distance was preventing.

### Cross-Domain ↔ History: Evolution of Warfare Toward Greater Distance and Abstraction

History shows a clear trend: warfare has progressively increased distance between killer and killed.

Pre-modern: hand-to-hand combat, close-range violence, direct visibility of enemy
Early modern: bows and arrows, crossbows, muskets — increasing distance gradually
Industrial: rifled muskets, artillery — dramatic distance increase
Modern: machine guns, tanks, aircraft — extreme distance
Contemporary: missiles, drones — ultimate distance and abstraction

The historical trend is not accident. At each step, the technology that increases distance is adopted preferentially, even when it is not superior militarily. This suggests: distance is preferred not for military advantage but for moral advantage.

The handshake: history shows that institutions systematically choose distance. Understanding this pattern enables recognition: the drive toward ever-greater distance technology is not inevitable. Alternative institutions could make different choices.

### Cross-Domain ↔ Creative-Practice: Narrative Distance and Moral Engagement

Narrative and creative practice operate at the level of perspective and distance. A story told from the protagonist's interior perspective (first person, or close third person) creates empathic engagement.

The same story told from an external perspective (distant third person, objective journalism) creates less empathic engagement. The distance in narrative creates distance in emotion.

The handshake: understanding how narrative creates empathic engagement through distance management offers institutional alternatives to warfare distance.

What if military institutions were designed around narrative that maintained the enemy's visibility and humanity? What if soldiers were required to know the names, stories, faces of those they killed? What if distance technology was constrained by narrative requirement to maintain visibility?

This is not naive pacifism. It is recognition that institutions can choose to design distance differently.

## Implementation Workflow: Recognizing Distance and Abstraction

**Diagnosis**: Where does your society kill from a distance? Where is technology used to abstract targets? Where is institutional dissociation preventing moral constraint?

Listen for language: "collateral damage," "surgical strike," "neutralize," "eliminate." These are abstractions. They enable distance.

**Interrogation**: What would happen if the abstraction was removed? If "collateral damage" was reframed as "we killed civilians including children," would the decision change?

Usually yes. Which reveals: the abstraction is doing moral work. The abstraction is enabling decisions that would be impossible if they were witnessed directly.

**Resistance**: Where can you insist on visibility? Where can you demand that consequences be witnessed? Where can you resist the institutional tendency toward distance?

## The Live Edge

### The Sharpest Implication

Your society probably commits atrocities enabled by distance technology. This is not new or special. Societies have used distance technology to enable harm for centuries.

But distance technology is accelerating. Drones, algorithms, automation — all are increasing distance and abstraction. Your society is moving toward forms of warfare where the killer has almost no visibility of the target.

This is progress in one sense: fewer soldiers die (the protected killer is safe). But it is regress in another sense: fewer moral constraints operate (the abstracted target does not trigger empathy).

### Generative Questions

- Where in your life are you abstracting people through distance? Where are you failing to witness the consequence of your actions?
- What institutional changes would be required to maintain moral visibility even in contexts of physical distance?
- Can technology be designed to resist abstraction? Can distance be maintained while visibility is preserved?
- What would it look like to require soldiers to know the people they kill? To know their names, their families, their stories?

## Connected Concepts

- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/enemy-as-abstraction|Enemy as Abstraction]] — the final step of abstraction through numbers and data
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/dehumanization-granularity|Dehumanization Granularity]] — the process that abstraction accelerates
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/propaganda-as-mirror|Propaganda as Mirror]] — institutional hiding of complicity through abstraction

## Open Questions

- Can we use distance technology without enabling abstraction? What would that require?
- Is the current trend toward greater distance technology inevitable? Or can societies choose alternatives?
- What would warfare look like if institutions were designed around maintaining visibility rather than enabling distance?

## Footnotes

[^1]: [[ARCHIVES/sources/Sam-Keen-Faces-of-the-Enemy|Keen, Faces of the Enemy]] — Part 1: "Technology and Distance" section; analysis of how technological distance enables abstraction and prevents empathic constraint
